claims.claim: The 1382 synod at the Black Friars and the earthquake, Vaughan's account: 'On the seventeenth of May, accordingly, a meeting was convened, consisting of eight prelates, fourteen doctors of civil and canon law, six bachelors of divinity, fifteen Mendicants, and four monks. The place of meeting was the residence of the Black Friars'; 'the synod had scarcely approached the matters to be adjusted by its wisdom, when the city was shaken with an earthquake, and the courage of some of the parties assembled was so much affected by that event, that they ventured to express their doubts, whether the object before them might not be displeasing to Heaven ... But the ready genius of Courtney gave a different meaning to the incident'; 'twenty-four conclusions were read'; 'ten of these conclusions were heretical, and the remaining were declared to be erroneous'. Courtenay archbishop: 'Courtney, bishop of London, was raised to the primacy' (October 1381). The quake itself is in Knighton under xii kal. Junii (21 May): 'terre motus generalis mala multa faciens in regno'. Vaughan's note gives a Gadstow Chronicle date about 30 May as 'probably a second convulsion'.
claims.witness: VAUGHAN (wyclif_tracts-and-treatises_vaughan1845.txt) l.3799-3800, 3808-3842, 3872-3876 (OCR 'witl^ut^ com', 'pubhcly', 'reahn'); KNIGHTON (knighton_chronicon-v2-lat_lumby1895.txt) l.16925-16929 (OCR 'mala An earth-' margin interleaved)

claims.claim: The twenty-four conclusions came from his writings: Shirley, 'twenty-four conclusions extracted from his writings were condemned'; F&M, 'twenty-four conclusions were pronounced some heretical and others erroneous'.
Vaughan admires him: he calls him 'the Reformer' throughout and writes 'his devout spirit passed to the world of rest'. Vaughan's edition: title page MDCCCXLV; preface dated February 1845.

Trialogus on the earthquake council and the earth crying out (Latin, told in modern words): 'fratres ... in suo concilio terraemotus Londoniis intoxicaverunt regnum nostrum'; 'sic in ista damnatione, ad ostendendum defectum attestationis humanae fuit insolite motus terrae. Quando enim membra Christi deficiunt ad reclamandum contra tales haereticos, terra clamat.' The 'heretici' are those who condemned his teaching on the sacrament ('isti haeretici tam expresse Christo contrarii', 'huius damnationis'), hence 'he wrote of his judges'. 'Trialogus' is a dialogue: Lechler quotes the colophon 'Explicit dyalogus'.
Lechler: the book was not written or finished before 1382: 'librum ante annum 1382 aut conscriptum aut certe absolutum non esse'; the editor is Gotthardus Lechler (title page), M DCCC LXIX.

Shirley edited the Fasciculi; it is a Carmelite collection hostile to Wyclif: title page 'ASCRIBED TO THOMAS NETTER OF WALDEN, PROVINCIAL OF THE CARMELITE ORDER IN ENGLAND'; its Latin narrative attacks him (e.g. the Ball story, l.23358-23395); the edition dated '1858' on the title page and 'April 26, 1858' at the end of Shirley's introduction.
Balliol: 'In April, and again in July 1361, Wyclif appears as master or warden of Balliol College, Oxford.' F&M: 'In April 1361 he was master of Balliol college'.

Bruges: 'a second embassy was appointed, to present a further and stronger remonstrance against these encroachments ... the second is that of John de Wycliffe ... Wycliffe reached that city in August, 1374'; the encroachments are benefices 'which, by means of this custom of provisors, had passed into the hands of foreigners'. F&M: 'The same year he was sent with others to Bruges to treat with the pope'.

Lutterworth from the crown: Shirley, Ludgershall exchanged 'again in 1374, on the presentation of the crown, for that of Lutterworth in Leicestershire, which he retained till his death', note 'April 7. Rot. pat. 48. Edward III.'; F&M, 'In April 1374 he was presented by the crown to the rectory of Lutterworth in Leicestershire'; Vaughan, after 'In November, 1375 ... About the same time the rectory of Lutterworth ... became vacant ... the royal patronage was again exercised in favour of Wycliffe'.
claims.witness: SHIRLEY l.2364-2389 (note l.2376-2377, OCR '.\piil 7.  lu>t. pat.'); F&M l.979-981; VAUGHAN l.1996-2004

claims.claim: St Paul's, February 1377: Vaughan, convocation summoned him 'to answer to the charge of holding and publishing certain erroneous and heretical opinions'; 'The nineteenth day of the same month was fixed for the hearing'; 'When Wycliffe presented himself to the convocation in St. Paul's, it was in company with John of Gaunt, and with Lord Percy'; Gaunt is 'the Duke of Lancaster' (l.2131). Shirley: 'on the 23d of February ... he came supported by the duke of Lancaster'; 'High words and eventually threats passed between the duke and the bishop of London; the council broke up in confusion'; the aim 'the humiliation of John of Gaunt'. F&M: 'In Feb. 1377 Wycliffe appeared before the convocation at St. Paul's to answer certain charges of false doctrine'.
claims.witness: VAUGHAN l.2122-2135; SHIRLEY l.1686-1698 (OCR 'Paurs', 'humihation'); F&M l.991-995

claims.claim: Papal letters, 1377: Vaughan, 'In the month of June, 1377, several letters were sent to England by the pontiff, concerning certain false and dangerous opinions said to be holden and promulgated by John de Wycliffe'; Vaughan names the pope of these years, 'Gregory the Eleventh then filled the papal chair'. Shirley: 'The bulls were issued from Rome on the 30th of May'. F&M: 'denounced from Rome in several papal bulls bearing date the 11 of this month'. Shirley's index: 'Bull of Gregory XI'.

1381, the sacrament: Shirley, 'he put out, in the spring of 1381, a paper containing twelve propositions, in which he denied the doctrine of transubstantiation'; 'it was condemned by the chancellor of the university and a select meeting of doctors'. Vaughan's gloss of transubstantiation's defence: 'an accident ... may be supposed to remain after the bread itself had ceased to exist'; Wyclif 'declares that the bread and wine remain in the sacrament after the consecration'.

The Latin confession in Vaughan's English: 'In the Latin confession, Wycliffe applies himself to demonstrate that "this venerable sacrament is naturally bread and wine, but sacramentally the body and blood of Christ."' Vaughan sets it before the Oxford assembly he dates November 1381 (a date that conflicts with his own sequence); the brief gives no date for it.

The rising of 1381: Vaughan, 'The summer of this year is memorable for the insurrection of the commons under Wat Tyler' (this year = 1381, after 'in the spring of 1381'). Knighton, hostile: 'Hic habuit praecursorem Johannem Balle veluti Christus Johannem Baptistam'. Ball a priest among the rebels: Shirley, 'John Balle, a fanatical priest who appeared among the leaders of the movement'. Vaughan: 'not the man to become the agent of insurrection, after the fashion of John Ball and Wat Tyler, as some of his ingenuous opponents have insinuated'.
claims.witness: VAUGHAN l.3661, 3798-3799, 7262-7264; KNIGHTON l.16943-16945 (OCR 'preecursorem', 'Balle?'); SHIRLEY l.2346-2348 (OCR 'BaHe', 'a})peared')

claims.claim: Knighton a Leicester chronicler, hostile: a manuscript title, 'Compilatio Henrici de Knyghton Canonici Abbathiae Leycestrensis de eventibus Angliae'; Lumby: Knighton 'may be drawing from sources in the house to which he belonged' (Leicester). Hostility: 'evangelica margarita spargitur et a porcis conculcatur'; 'Hic multas dicitur introducere in ecclesia opiniones que a catholicis ecclesiae doctoribus reprobantur'.
Knighton on the translation: 'Hic magister Johannes Wyclif Evangelium ... transtulit de Latino in Anglicam linguam non angelicam'.
claims.witness: KNIGHTON l.16947-16965 (OCR, margin 'Wycliffe translated the Scrip- English' interleaved)

claims.claim: The New Testament probably Wyclif's: F&M, 'This translation might probably be the work of Wycliffe himself; at least the similarity of style between the Gospels and the other parts favours the supposition.'

The Old Testament and Hereford: F&M, 'the Old Testament was taken in hand by one of Wycliffe's coadjutors ... A second copy ... has a note at the end, assigning the translation to Nicholas de Hereford. This note was evidently made not very long after the Ms. was written'; 'both these copies end abruptly in the book of Baruch'; 'nor is it unreasonable to conjecture further, that the cause of the interruption was the summons which Hereford received to appear before the synod in 1382'; 'completed by a different hand, and not improbably by Wycliffe himself'. Pollard: 'the books of the Old Testament, as far as Daniel, are stated on contemporary authority to have been rendered by Nicholas Hereford'.

Purvey and the later version: F&M, 'it may therefore be regarded as undeniable, that Purvey was also the author of the General Prologue, and consequently of the later version of the Bible, to which it belongs'; Purvey 'lived with Wycliffe in his later years'. Pollard: 'A revised edition, usually assigned to Wyclif's friend, John Purvey, was completed a few years later'; the argument for Purvey 'lamentably weak'.

Pollard, 1903 (title page l.111): 'historians, after salving their conscience by confessing that there is substantially no evidence for attributing the rest of the work to Wyclif, wherever they have afterwards to mention it, invariably connect it with his name'; the OT 'far more likely that it was taken up by some other of Wyclif's numerous disciples at Oxford rather than by the master himself'; 'enough if he inspired others to work at this great task'.
F&M edited the Wycliffite Bible in 1850: preface dated 'British Museum, 1st October, 1850'.

Death: Shirley, 'On the 29th of December of the same year, as he was hearing mass in his parish church a fatal stroke deprived him of speech, and on the 31st he breathed his last' (his 'same year' follows an OCR or print slip '1381' for the citation year); F&M, 'until death interrupted his occupations on the last day of December 1384'; Vaughan, 'he is said to have been employed in administering the bread of the eucharist, when assailed by his last sickness. The paralysis which then seized him deprived him at once of utterance if not of consciousness. This happened on the twenty-ninth of December, [year garbled], and on the thirty-first day of that month'.
claims.witness: SHIRLEY l.2743-2751; F&M l.1028-1031 (OCR 'occu- pations'); VAUGHAN l.4760-4766 (year OCR '_J^_SsA')

claims.claim: Walsingham, hostile, St Albans monk (title page 'QUONDAM MONACHI S. ALBANI'): 'Die Sancti Thomae, Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi et Martyris, organum diabolicum, hostis Ecclesiae ... Johannes de Wiclif, dum in Sanctum Thomam, ut dicitur, eodem die in sua praedicatione quam dicere praeparaverat, orationes et blasphemias vellet evomere, repente judicio Dei percussus, sensit paralysim omnia membra sua generaliter invasisse'; 'ut ferunt hii qui affuerunt morienti, per signa forinseca moriens desperavit'.

Summons by Urban VI and the letter: Vaughan, 'Wycliffe was summoned by Urban to appear at Rome ... His declining health afforded sufficient ground for his refusing compliance'; the Latin, headed 'A.D. M.CCC.LXXXIV': 'Gaudeo plane detegere cuicunque fidem meam quam teneo, et specialiter Romano pontifici: quia suppono quod si sit orthodoxa, ipse fidem illam humiliter confirmabit, et si sit erronea, emendabit'; 'Ex istis elicio, tanquam consilium, quod papa dimittat seculari brachio dominium temporale'. Arnold names the pope Urban VI: 'missae Papae Urbano VI.'
claims.witness: VAUGHAN l.4642-4645 (OCR 'gTound'); SHIRLEY l.27355-27371, 27415-27416 (OCR 'cuiciinqiie', 'Komano', 'iijse', 'con- nnnabit', 'tanquaiii consiliuui'); ARNOLD3 (wyclif_select-english-works-v3_arnold1871.txt) l.30715-30725

claims.claim: Arnold on the English form of the letter: 'The English version ... is a heightened and amplified composition; probably it was prepared by Wyclif's followers chiefly with a view to home consumption'; 'Of the authenticity of the letter there can be no doubt ... It was written therefore in 1384'. Arnold is the editor (title page 'THOMAS ARNOLD, M.A.').

Birth: Vaughan, 'The biographers of Wycliffe all mention the year 1324 as that of his birth. The place of his nativity still bears his name, a village about six miles from the town of Richmond in Yorkshire'; F&M, 'John Wycliffe, according to his biographers, was born near Richmond in Yorkshire, in the year 1324'; Shirley, 'perhaps the earliest notice is in his biography by Lewis, who says that he was born, very probably, about the year 1324. This vague conjecture ... has been accepted by some later writers as a positive date'; his writings 'give an idea of greater age than Lewis' date would assign'.
claims.witness: VAUGHAN l.576-578 (OCR 'TieaB liis name-^a village^a^bout', 'RiGlimond', 'Yorksliire'); F&M l.933-953; SHIRLEY l.654-660, 727-728 (OCR 'LcJwis', 'jjreater ajje')

claims.claim: Livings: F&M, Fillingham 1361, exchanged for Ludgershall 'in Nov. 1368'; Vaughan, 'Fylingham'.

Doctor of theology: Knighton, 'doctor in theologia eminentissimus in diebus illis. In philosophia nulli reputabatur secundus'; Shirley, 'There is documentary evidence that Wyclif was a doctor of divinity in 1374'.
Lollards: Vaughan, 'With a view also to increase the odium so freely cast upon the disciples of the Reformer, they were now designated Lollards'.
F&M on the versions: 'In the interval between the years 1382 and 1526 they diffused a great amount of scriptural truth'.

Hus's sermon: Workman and Pope, 'In a sermon before the Synod and in the presence of Zbinek (probably in June 1408), Hus had stated: "I could hope that my soul should be where rests the soul of Wyclif."' Edition dated 1904 (title page, 'PATERNOSTER ROW 1904').
Schaff, 1915 (title page l.143): 'Huss appropriated paragraph after paragraph from his predecessor and transferred them often with little verbal change to his own pages.'

Constance, session of Saturday 4 May [1415]: 'Concilium pronunciat haereticum Joannem Wicleff, ac memoriam ejusdem condemnat, & mandat exhumari ossa ipsius'; 'declarat, diffinit et sententiat eumdem Joannem Wicleff fuisse notorium haereticum, pertinacem, ac in haeresi decessisse ... decernitque et ordinat, corpus & ejus ossa, si ab aliis fidelibus corporibus discerni possint, exhumari'. The year from 'Die secunda Maji, mccccxv' a few entries earlier.
Martin V: 'Papst Martin V.: Verurteilung von Wyclef und Huss (1418). Bulle "Inter cunctas", 22. Febr. 1418'.

Thorpe's tribute, Pollard's modernised text: 'Master John Wyclif was holden of full many men, the greatest Clerk [Divine] that they knew then living; and therewith he was named a passing ruly man and an innocent in his living'. Thorpe was examined before 'Thomas Arundell, Archbishop of Canterbury' in 1407.
claims.witness: POLLARD l.7204-7208 (OCR 'Wyclipfb', 'raely'; Pollard's bracket '[Divine]' and a page head fall inside the sentence; the card quotes only up to 'Clerk'), 270-272, 1013

claims.claim: Vaughan, 'Gospel Doctor': 'his manner of inculcating religious truth on the sole authority of Scripture ... secured him the honourable appellation of the "Gospel Doctor."' Lechler's manuscript colophon: 'sacre Theologie professore doctoreque evangelico Nacionis anglicane'.

Foxe: 'he himself, forty-one years after his death, was taken out of his grave and burned'; 'which ashes they also took and threw into the river'; 'for though they digged up his body, burnt his bones, and drowned his ashes, yet the word of God ... they could not burn'; heading 'TO BE BURNED FORTY-ONE YEARS AFTER HE WAS BURIED IN HIS OWN PARISH AT LUTTERWORTH. A. D. 1425.' Editors' notes: 'See the edition of 1563, p. 105, and the Latin edition of 1559, p. 23'; 'The bones of Wickliff were not yet commanded by the council of Constance to be burned.' Edition title page MDCCCXXXVII.
Shirley: 'If considered only as the father of English prose, the great reformer might claim more reverential treatment at our hands.'

Matthew on De Officio Pastorali: 'De Officio Pastorali and De Papa (Shirley 61 and 62) are undoubtedly genuine'; the tract: 'the freris wit þer fautours seyn þat it is heresye to write þus goddis lawe in english, & make it knowun to lewid men'; '& þus crist & his apostlis tauȝten þe puple in þat tunge þat was moost knowun to þe puple' (OCR cleaned; the file prints thorn and yogh as OCR garbles). Matthew's edition 1880 (l.146).
claims.witness: MATTHEW (wyclif_english-works-hitherto-unprinted_matthew1880.txt) l.2866-2867, 35750-35753 (OCR 'a nt heer^ "be freris wit \\>er fautours seyn \\>at it is heresye ... knowui^ ... lewid me?^'), 35792-35793 (OCR 'j^us crist & his apostlis taujtew fe puple in fat tuwge fat was moost knoAvuw to J^e puple'), 146

claims.claim: Shirley on the early Oxford claims: Queen's, 'No such list, however, can be discovered'; the Merton fellow 'was, almost certainly, another man of the same name, who died rector of a living in Sussex in 1383'; Canterbury Hall 'fuller evidence compels us now to surrender as belonging, of historical right, to another'. Vaughan: 'At the age of sixteen, we find him entered as a commoner in Queen's College, Oxford. This was in 1340'; 'Merton, to which he shortly afterwards removed'; 'four years later we find the name of John de Wycliffe as that of the person filling the office of warden in Canterbury Hall'. F&M: Queen's, Merton, and 'In December 1365 he was appointed by abp. Islip warden of Canterbury Hall'.

Whether he appeared at the 1382 synod: Shirley, 'Wyclif himself was never summoned before the council'; F&M, 'According to Knighton, Wycliffe appeared both before the synod at the Preaching Friars, and before this convocation ... But from his name not occurring in the documents of the archiepiscopal register ... it seems more probable that he had previously withdrawn himself'.

Banished from the university and last years at Lutterworth: Shirley, 'he himself was banished from the university'; Lutterworth 'which he retained till his death'; Vaughan, 'Henceforward he is found amidst his duties at Lutterworth'; F&M, 'It is certain that his last years were spent there'.

The rising, Carmelite and Walsingham sides: Fasciculi narrative, Ball 'confitebatur publice eis quod per biennium erat discipulus Wycclyff, et ab eo didicerat haereses quas docuit' at St Albans; Walsingham, 'multis opinantibus propter remissam curam Archiepiscopi, caeterorumque comprovincialium Episcoporum ... filios suos, Johannem Wyclif et ejus sequaces'.

Knighton's authorship: a manuscript title 'Compilatio Henrici de Knyghton Canonici Abbathiae Leycestrensis'; Shirley, 'See especially pseudo-Knighton'; 'we learn from the so-called Knighton ... but it is not easy to assign the true date to them, the more so as the chronicler himself does not understand them'. Lumby speaks of 'the compiler of Knighton'.

De civili dominio, his first principle: 'prima, quod nemo ut est in peccato mortali habet iusticiam simpliciter ad donum Dei' (no one, as he is in mortal sin, has a true right to God's gift); Poole's note: 'the wicked have, properly speaking, no lordship'

The 1377 bulls, Shirley: 'The bulls were issued from Rome on the 30th of May'; 'another addressed to the university of Oxford, prohibiting the nineteen conclusions it condemned from being held within the university, and commanding the chancellor to arrest Wyclif, and bring him before the archbishop and bishop of London' (OCR 'bnlls', 'univei^sity')

Knighton, hostile, on the English gospel: 'Hic magister Johannes Wyclif Evangelium ... transtulit de Latino in Anglicam linguam non angelicam, unde per ipsum fit vulgare et magis apertum laicis, et mulieribus legere scientibus ... et sic evangelica margarita spargitur et a porcis conculeatur [OCR, conculcatur]' (made it common and more open to lay people and to women who can read; the gospel pearl is scattered and trodden by swine)

sides: Josiah Forshall and Frederic Madden (1850): the New Testament 'might probably be the work of Wycliffe himself'; the first Old Testament begun by Nicholas Hereford (an early note), breaking off in Baruch, 'completed by a different hand, and not improbably by Wycliffe himself'; John Purvey 'undeniable' author of the General Prologue and later version (F&M l.2319, 2407-2420, 4071-4075)

Alfred W. Pollard (1903): Hereford's books 'as far as Daniel'; 'substantially no evidence for attributing the rest of the work to Wyclif'; more likely 'some other of Wyclif's numerous disciples at Oxford'; the Purvey argument 'lamentably weak' (POLLARD l.841-848, 949, 968-972)
Henry Knighton, hostile contemporary: Wyclif himself 'Evangelium ... transtulit de Latino in Anglicam linguam' (KNIGHTON l.16947-16965)

contested_claims.claim: How and where he was struck on 29 December 1384
sides: Shirley (1858): 'as he was hearing mass in his parish church' (SHIRLEY l.2748-2749)
Vaughan (1845): 'he is said to have been employed in administering the bread of the eucharist' (VAUGHAN l.4761-4763)
Walsingham, hostile: struck 'judicio Dei' as he meant to preach against St Thomas on his feast; died in despair 'ut ferunt hii qui affuerunt' (WALSINGHAM l.10997-11041)
Vaughan and F&M: his biographers give 1324 (VAUGHAN l.576-577; F&M l.933-953)
Shirley: a 'vague conjecture' of Lewis; his writings suggest greater age (SHIRLEY l.654-660, 727-728)

contested_claims.claim: Date of the crown's presentation to Lutterworth
sides: Shirley and F&M: April 1374 (patent roll, 7 April), before Bruges (SHIRLEY l.2364-2377; F&M l.979-981)
Vaughan: about the same time as November 1375 (VAUGHAN l.1996-2004)

contested_claims.claim: Any link between Wyclif and the rising of 1381
sides: Hostile witnesses allege it: Knighton (Ball his forerunner, KNIGHTON l.16943-16945); the Carmelite narrative of the Fasciculi (Ball confessed two years as his disciple, SHIRLEY l.23358-23387); Walsingham (the bishops' laxity toward Wyclif and his followers, WALSINGHAM l.2183-2194)
Shirley: Ball 'confessed, or was said to have confessed' (SHIRLEY l.2346-2350); Vaughan: Wyclif 'not the man to become the agent of insurrection' (VAUGHAN l.7262-7264)

contested_claims.claim: Date and aim of the St Paul's hearing, February 1377
sides: Vaughan: 19 February, to answer 'erroneous and heretical opinions' (VAUGHAN l.2122-2128)
Shirley: 23 February; its aim 'the humiliation of John of Gaunt' (SHIRLEY l.1686-1698)
F&M: Feb. 1377, 'certain charges of false doctrine' (F&M l.991-995)
Shirley: issued 30 May (SHIRLEY l.1728-1729)
F&M: dated 11 June (F&M l.995-996)
Vaughan: sent in June (VAUGHAN l.2252-2253)

contested_claims.claim: Whether he appeared before the 1382 synod
sides: Knighton, as F&M report: he appeared and gave a profession on the eucharist (F&M l.1019-1022)
Shirley: never summoned (SHIRLEY l.2696-2697); F&M: more probably withdrawn, since the register does not name him (F&M l.1022-1026)

contested_claims.claim: His early Oxford years: Queen's commoner, Merton fellow, warden of Canterbury Hall
sides: Vaughan and F&M: all three are his (VAUGHAN l.662-664, 745, 1270-1273; F&M l.953-962)
Shirley: no Queen's list exists; the Merton fellow and the Canterbury Hall warden were another John Wyclif (SHIRLEY l.737-805, 870-871, 972-977)

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Leicester chronicle's account of Wyclif is Henry Knighton's
sides: A manuscript title and Lumby's 1895 edition: Henry Knighton, canon of Leicester Abbey (KNIGHTON l.1427-1428)
Shirley: 'pseudo-Knighton', 'the so-called Knighton', a chronicler who does not understand the Oxford proceedings (SHIRLEY l.2369, 2722-2730)

absent_details.detail: His parents and family
absent_details.note: No source used here names them. Vaughan says his writings show no intercourse with his kindred; Shirley infers only that he belonged to the family of Wycliffe-on-Tees (VAUGHAN l.648-655; SHIRLEY note l.694-700). Not told.

absent_details.note: The census year c.1330 appears only in Library file headers (VAUGHAN l.3; TRIALOGUS l.2; MATTHEW l.2); no text line gives it. Not used.

absent_details.note: Foxe gives 'forty-one years after his death', the heading 'A.D. 1425' and 'the river' (FOXE3 l.7915-7923, 7990-7992, 8031-8034); the dossier's searches for '1428', 'Fleming' and 'Swift' across cic/texts found nothing. The card gives Foxe's words only.

absent_details.note: Shirley: 'No friendly hand has left us any, even the slightest, memorial of the life and death of the great reformer' (SHIRLEY l.2753-2755). Walsingham's volume I, which covered 1377-78, is not held.

claims.claim: Choir scene, Kempis's own memory in the Life of Florentius, Arthur's English: 'At that time I used to go into the Choir with the other scholars as I was ordered to do by Master John Boheme, who ruled the Scholars and Choristers strictly. And as often as I saw my Master Florentius standing there — though he did not look round — I was careful not to chatter, for I was awed by his presence'; 'Once on a time it happened when I was standing near him in the Choir that he turned to share our book for the chanting, and he, standing behind me, put his hands upon my shoulder — but I stood still, hardly daring to move, bewildered with gratification at so great an honour.' The canons of Deventer: 'There were then in the Chapter of Deventer divers Canons and Vicars'. The text says 'shoulder' (singular); the brief keeps it.

Florentius was vicar of Deventer: 'that most reverend man Master Florentius, who was Vicar of the Church of Deventer, a devout priest'. Busch: 'dominus Fiorencius Radewin Daventriensis vicarius' (OCR 'Fiorencius'). The brief's form is the census voice 'Florens Radewijns'; Kempis's English calls him Florentius.

The Lives as a memorial: 'Now since many Fathers and devout brethren, who were of old well known to me, are fallen asleep, I fear not to speak of their virtues, that by so doing I may leave a good memorial of them to those that come after'. Written as a dialogue: Arthur, '"The Lives" are written in the form of a dialogue between an elder Brother of the house and a Novice'. Arthur's title: 'The Founders of the New Devotion'; 'the movement known as "The New Devotion"' (CHRON 237-238).

Grote began the movement: Busch, 'magister Gerardus Magnus origo fuit et pater primus omnium hominum moderne devocionis huius patrie' (OCR 'omni- um'); Kempis, Chronicle part II ch. V, after Gerard's death 'the devotion of faithful persons in Deventer, Zwolle, Kampen and the neighbouring towns began to grow mightily'. Death 1384: 'In the year of the Lord 1384, on the Feast day of the blessed Bernard the Abbot ... Gerard, surnamed Groote, died at Deventer'. 'Low Countries' is the census region; Kempis names Holland, Gelders, Brabant (FOUNDERS 3790-3793).

Name and birthplace, Kempis's own Chronicle under 1406: 'Thomas Hemerken of the city of Kempen in the diocese of Cologne, and own brother to John of Kempen the first Prior. The father of these was called John and their mother Gertrude.' The death notice: 'died our most beloved Brother Thomas Hemerken, who was born in the city of Kempen, in the diocese of Cologne.' In 1399 he calls himself 'I, Thomas of Kempen'.

About a year in the brothers' house at Deventer: 'by the aid and counsel of Florentius, I also took up my abode in this house, and continued in the Community for about a year, having Arnold as my companion, for we were content to share one little cell and bed. Here indeed I learned to write, to read the Holy Scripture'; 'All that I was then able to earn by writing I gave for the expenses of the Community'. Earlier Florentius 'kept me for a while with him in his house ... and he placed me in the School, and besides this gave me the books which he thought I needed'.

claims.claim: 1399, own words: 'In the year 1399, Indulgences were granted to the people of Zwolle by the Apostolic See, and Pope Boniface the Ninth granted these to be gained by all that were truly penitent at the Church of St. Michael'; 'In this same year, I, Thomas of Kempen, a scholar at Deventer and a native of the diocese of Cologne, came to Zwolle to gain indulgences. Then I went on, glad at heart, to Mount St. Agnes, and was instant to be allowed there to abide, and I was received with mercy.' The brief's 'pardons the pope had granted' tells 'Indulgences ... by the Apostolic See' in modern words.

Mount St Agnes new, outside Zwolle, and its first prior John: 'In the year 1399, after Easter, John of Kempen, one of the community at Windesem, was chosen to be Prior of the House of Mount St. Agnes'; 'The House of Mount St. Agnes, which lieth outside the walls of the town of Zwolle'. 'Canons regular' as clergy under a rule: the Chronicle's own title, 'The Chronicle of the Canons Regular of Mount St. Agnes', and Busch's Rule of the Canons Regular of St Augustine (Arthur, FOUNDERS 1196-1197).

Clothed as a canon in 1406: 'In the year of the Lord 1406, on the Feast of Corpus Christi, which fell in that year on the day before the Feast of St. Barnabas, two brothers that were Clerks, and one that was a Convert, were invested. These were Thomas Hemerken ...'. The notice: 'From this same brother he received his investiture after six years of probation'. 'Clothed as a canon' tells 'invested' in modern words.

The dream of 1424 in the Chronicle (dreamer unnamed): 'In the year of the Lord 1424, on the Saturday following the Feast of St. Andrew, being the second of December, the venerable Father John Huesden, who was the second Prior of Windesem, died'; 'Now it came to pass a few days before his death, and within the Octave of St. Martin the Bishop, that two Brothers came from Mount St. Agnes to Windesem to commune with the Prior. And one of them had a dream after this wise, which vision did foretell the Prior's death'. The Chronicle spells him 'John Vos of Huesden' (heading) and 'Huesden'; the brief uses 'Heusden', Busch's and the scan's form ('lohannes Huesden' in Busch's OCR at 4803; 'Vos de Huesden').

Busch names the dreamer: 'Contigit ante paucos dies sui obitus, ut duo fratres notabiles de Monte sancte Agnetis prope ZuoUis ordinis nostri dictum priorem nostrum super certis rebus consulturi in Windesem advenirent, quorum unus frator Thomas de Kerapis vir probate vite, qui plures devotos tractatulos composuit, videlicet „qui sequitur me" de imitacione Christi cum aliis, nocte insecuta sompnium vidit presagium futuronim.' (OCR 'frator' for frater, 'Kerapis' for Kempis, 'futuronim' for futurorum, 'ZuoUis' for Zwollis). Told in modern words, no quotation marks. Margin date '2.Dec U24.' (OCR for 1424) at l.5345.

Busch a canon of Windesheim of Thomas's day: Arthur, 'John Buschius, a younger contemporary of a Kempis'; Busch writes 'A me autem in Windesem pro tunc simplici fratre ... ista sunt inchoata, sed in Sultensi prelatura ... anno domini millesimo quadringentesimo sexagesimo 1464 ... completa' (OCR 'quadringentesirao', 'i464').

Atkynson and Gerson: Ingram, 'The second is the work of Dr. William Atkynson; it was executed at the desire of Margaret, Countess of Richmond and Derby, the mother of King Henry the Seventh'; 'printed, along with Atkynson's version of the three preceding Books, by Wynkyn de Worde in 1504'; 'Atkynson ... speaks of the work as "compyled in Latin by the right worshypfulle doctor master Iohn Gerson," and as "the boke of Iohn Gerson, Chaunceler of Paris" ... actually names Gerson in the text of his translation in II. ix ... as "the auctour of this treatyse." I think him quite mistaken in this'. (OCR 'liichmond', 'Seventli', 'AV^orde', 'lohfi', 'tliis'.)

Benham: 'THE authorship of the following treatise is commonly attributed to Thomas Kempis. There seems no doubt that this must be a mistake'; 'He then began copying some pious and ascetic treatises, among them the Imitatio Christi. To this he appended the same note as that at the end of the Bible, and thence arose the erroneous notion that he was its author'; 'there seems strong reason for accepting the belief that the writer of the Imitatio was John Gersen, who is called John of Cavaglia, and that he was an Abbot of Vercelli'. Benham also concedes 'our ground becomes somewhat uncertain'. Benham's view, not settled.

claims.claim: Ingram for Thomas: 'I believe neither in the authorship of the Chancellor Gerson, nor in that of Gersen (who, indeed, appears to be an apocryphal person) ; I am convinced that, in the words of Hirsche, "Thomas und kein Anderer der Verfasser der Imitatio ist"'. Ingram's view.

Brother John's death: Chronicle ch. XXIV, 'In the same year, on the fourth day of November, at midnight, died Brother John of Kempen ... being in the sixty-seventh year of his age'; 'I was with him and I closed his eyes, for I had been sent by the Visitors to bear him company, and I abode with him for a year and two months.' 'In the same year' follows ch. XXIII, headed 'In the year of our Lord 1422 (1432)'; the next entry is 1433. 'Aged' tells 'sixty-seventh year' and 'in a good old age'.

Death notice, by another brother: 'SO FAR THE CHRONICLE WAS WRITTEN BY THOMAS OF KEMPEN; THE RESIDUE THEREOF WAS DONE BY ANOTHER.' 'In the same year, on the Feast of St. James the Less, and after Compline, died our most beloved Brother Thomas Hemerken ... He was in the ninety-second year of his age, and this was the sixty-third year after his investiture; likewise he had been a Priest for above fifty-seven years.' 'Moreover, he wrote that complete copy of the Bible which we use, and also many other books for the use of the House, and for sale. Likewise he composed divers little books for the edification of the young, which books were plain and simple in style, but mighty in the matter thereof and in their effectual operation.' 'The thought of the Lord's passion filled his heart with love, and he was wondrous comfortable to the troubled and the tempted'. The year 1471 is from the preceding entry, 'In the year of the Lord 1471'.

Close, own words of the Deventer brothers: 'Never before could I recollect to have seen such men, so devout and fervent were they in the love of God and of their neighbour.' (in the Life of John Gronde).

Exile of 1429: 'In the year of the Lord 1429 ... heavy threats were made against the Regulars in that they obeyed the letter of the Apostolic See'; 'they were driven either to begin again to sing the services of the church or to depart from the country'; 'by command of the Apostolic See'; 'the second was Brother Thomas of Kempen, the Sub-Prior'; they took ship 'for Frisia meaning to go to their Brothers at Lunenkerc'. 'A papal interdict, a ban on church services' tells 'the Interdict' that halted the singing of the services. Kept to card.

Sub-prior again in 1448: 'In the year of the Lord 1448'; 'Brother Thomas of Kempen was nominated and elected after a brief scrutiny. He was one of the elders, being sixty-seven years of age, and in past times had been appointed to this office'. Scully: 'For many years the Venerable Thomas à Kempis had charge of the young Religious at Mount St. Agnes. The office of training the Novices was with the Windesheimers usually attached to the sub-priorship'; 'Twice Thomas was elected Sub-Prior' (OCR '&' for 'à', drop-cap 'F' lost: 'OR many years').

Neale: 'Here it was that, in 1400, Thomas a Kempis was transferred'; 'A Bible of his writing is still extant, in four volumes, folio ; begun in 1417, and finished in 1459'; 'that work which, next to the Holy Scriptures, has probably been read more widely than any other in the Western Church'; 'It is now, however, almost a settled point among ecclesiastical scholars, that Thomas was not its author' (side-heading 'not ihe' run into the line by OCR); 'the only reason for ascribing it to him consists in the epigraph, "Finished and completed in the year of our Lord 1441, by the hands of brother Thomas a Kempis, of the monastery of Mount Saint Agnes, near ZwoUe." The same reason might make him author of the Bible itself.' Neale's preface is dated 'Nov. 20, 1857'; the card's 'writing in the 1850s' rests on that line.

Birth year: Benham, 'Thomas Hemercker was born at Kempen, near Koln, about the year 1380'; Scully, 'he was born the same year, 1380'; Duthoit, 'He was born in 1380'. Ingram reports a 17th-century hand in the Dublin manuscript: 'Tho. e Kempis natus 1380 obyt 25 Julij 1471. aiio set : 92 :' (OCR).

Benham, 'His father was a labouring man, and his mother the village schoolmistress.' Neither cites a source.

Benham on the Bible: 'He was employed fifteen years in transcribing a Bible in four vols., folio, which Rosweide saw in the library of the canons regular of Koln, with the following note which Kempis had appended : — "Finitus et completus Anno Domini MCCCCXXXix. per manus fratris Thomas Kempis."'

Arthur: 'the present writer has seen a MS. of the first book of the "Imitatio," whose date would seem to be about 1423, in which that work is assigned to a Carthusian Monk.' Arthur on Thomas's priesthood under Vorniken: 'those years in which he composed the first part at least of the great work with which his name is associated.'

Lee and Hilton, reported by Ingram: 'Volume II. of the second edition (1710) of the Christian Pattern contains a translation of some of the minor writings of Thomas'; the translator 'seems beyond doubt to have been ... Dr. Francis Lee'; 'he raises the question whether the Imitation is not really the work of an Englishman, Walter Hilton, author of the Scale (or Ladder) of Perfection'; the idea came from Charles Hatton's letter 'dated December 2, 1706'. 'Early 1700s' rests on these two dates.

Pohl: 'Puyol non Thomam Kempensem, sed suum Ioannem Gersen, quem ne fuisse quidem umquam persuasum habemus, praestantissimos De imitatione Christi libros scripsisse opinatus' (OCR 'Kem- pensem', 'loannem'). Pohl's editorship: Duthoit's title, 'translated from the text of the edition of Michael Joseph Pohl'; the file names him Josef Pohl.

Grube's note on the dream passage: 'Die folgende Stelle hat das Chron. Montis St. Agnetis S. 50 entlehnt.' (The Chronicle of Mount St Agnes, p. 50, borrowed the following passage.) Grube's view, given as his.

Lydwine: Scully, 'our venerable Author contented himself with merely editing the biography already published by one John Brugman. A comparison with the latter shows that almost throughout a Kempis has retained even the language of Brugman.' Prologue: 'Brother N., a poor pilgrim'. Arthur: 'There is little doubt, however, that it is an authentic work of a Kempis, as a copy of it exists in his own handwriting'; 'a dedication ascribing it to "Frater N pauper peregrinus," but this may easily refer to Thomas himself.'

Exercises, versio prima, second week: 'Pro secunda hebdómada et deinceps multum expediet interdum legere libellos aliquot deuotos, ut librum de Imitatione Christi vel euangelia vel uitas sanctorum.' Burgos: 'ex translatione antiquissima, Burgis, in Hispania edita anno 1516'; its title 'Contemptus mundi, compuesto por el famoso maestro en sancta theologia Juan Gerson, chanceller de París.' 'The little Gerson' renders 'Gerconzito' in modern words.

Wesley: 'When I was about twenty-two, my father pressed me to enter into holy orders. At the same time, the providence of God directing me to Kempis's Christian Pattern, I began to see that true religion was seated in the heart'; 'I was, however, very angry at Kempis for being too strict'.

claims.claim: Benham: 'Whoever the author may be, he has produced the most popular religious work in Christendom.' Busch: 'vir probate vite' (a man of proven life).

The Chronicle's continuation and range: Arthur, 'The last nine pages of the Latin text have been added by an anonymous writer, and carry on the chronicle from the year 1471, in which a Kempis died, to 1477 ... and contains a notice of the author written by a contemporary member of the community'. Preface: 'I have gathered together a few things out of many, and these I have seen with mine own eyes, or have heard from the Elders of our House, or else have gathered from the writings of others.' Chapter I tells 'how Master Gerard Groote first pointed out this place to them'.

Who sent him: the notice, 'In the days of his youth he was an hearer of Florentius at Deventer, by whom also he was sent, when twenty years old, to his own brother, who at that time was Prior of Mount St. Agnes.' His own entry has him come to Zwolle and go on to ask to stay (CHRON 1103-1106). Benham, 'In 1399 he entered as a novice among the canons regular of Mount S. Agnes'.

The Imitation as four books: Benham's title, 'The Imitation of Christ: Four Books'; Ingram, in the autograph there is not 'anything to show that the four Books (commonly so called) are portions of a single work'. The card keeps 'four books' as Benham's title.
Busch a canon of Windesheim: he professed at Windesheim on 6 January 1420 in Grube's account ('am 6. Januar 1419 eingekleidet und am gleichen Tage des folgenden Jahres zur Profess zugelassen').

contested_claims.claim: Who wrote the Imitation of Christ
sides: Thomas: Johannes Busch, a Windesheim canon of his day, names 'frator Thomas de Kerapis' (OCR) as author of the treatise 'qui sequitur me' de imitacione Christi (BUSCH l.5413-5415); John Ingram is 'convinced' with Hirsche (INGRAM l.1182-1186); Josef Pohl rejects Puyol's Gersen (POHL l.18009-18015); J. P. Arthur says Thomas composed 'the first part at least' (CHRON l.255-258); the Jesuit editors of the Exercises (IGN l.2643-2644)

The 1441 copy in his hand: Ingram's 'autograph of 1441' (INGRAM l.175, 246); John Mason Neale quotes its colophon and holds it the only ground for the attribution, which 'might make him author of the Bible itself' (NEALE l.4731-4736)

John Gerson, chancellor of Paris: William Atkynson's English version, printed 1504 (INGRAM l.166-177, 1175-1182); the Burgos edition of 1516 (IGN l.3072-3073, 3101-3102); Ignatius's 'Gerconzito' (IGN l.2604-2605)
John Gersen, abbot of Vercelli: William Benham, who says Thomas's copying note began 'the erroneous notion' (BENHAM l.487-490, 511-521, 628-633)
A Carthusian monk: a manuscript of book one of about 1423 that J. P. Arthur saw (FOUNDERS l.1517-1524)
Walter Hilton: Francis Lee's question, as John Ingram reports it, and rejects it (INGRAM l.310-322, 398-410)
Against Thomas, without a candidate: John Mason Neale, 'almost a settled point among ecclesiastical scholars, that Thomas was not its author' (NEALE l.4719-4723)

absent_details.note: His Chronicle records no ordination of his (searched 'ordained', 'priesthood', 'holy orders'). The death notice gives 'above fifty-seven years' as a priest in 1471 (CHRON l.3417). William Duthoit's 1413 (DUTHOIT l.741-743) has no cited source. Kept to the card.

claims.claim: The flight, Office Legenda Lection I in Comper's English: 'Hence, after he had returned from Oxford to his father's house, he said one day to his sister ... ‘My beloved sister, thou hast two tunics which I greatly covet, one white and the other grey. Therefore I ask thee if thou wilt kindly give them to me, and bring them me to-morrow to the wood near by, together with my father's rain-hood.’'; 'he straightway cut off the sleeves from the grey tunic and the buttons from the white'; 'he covered his head with the rain-hood aforesaid, so that thus in some measure ... he might present a certain likeness to a hermit'; 'cried: ‘My brother is mad! My brother is mad!’ Whereupon he drove her from him with threats, and fled himself at once without delay'. Told as the Office's account (hagiographic).

claims.claim: Horstman's edition dated 1895 in-text: Comper cites 'Yorkshire Writers. Ed. by C. Horstman (Swan Sonnenschein & Co., 1895), vol. ii. p. xxxv.'

Yorkshire and Thornton: Office 'born in the village of Thornton, near Pickering, in the diocese of York'; Horstman 'at Thornton (now Thornton Dale), a village ... E. of Pickering, at the foot of the hills in the North Riding of Yorkshire'.

Oxford: 'Master Thomas Neville, at one time Archdeacon of Durham, honourably maintained him in the University of Oxford'; 'At length, in his nineteenth year ...'. Horstman 'in his rot [19th, OCR] year ... left the University'.

John de Dalton: 'a certain worthy squire, named John de Dalton'; Lection IV 'he, at his own expense, clad him according to his wish, — with clothing suitable for a hermit; and kept him for a long time in his own house, giving him a place for his solitary abode'. The preaching: 'having first besought the blessing of the priest, he went into the preacher's pulpit and gave the people a sermon'.

Not in holy orders: Horstman 'R. Rolle himself belonged to no monastic institution, was not in holy orders, was neither priest nor monk, and consequently was not allowed to preach from the pulpit'; footnote 'It is erroneous to call R. Rolle a famous preacher'.

Chantry priest: Forshall and Madden 'This was the work of Richard Rolle, chantry priest at' ... 'Hampole near Doncaster, who died in 1349.' (OCR has split the sentence: l.439 then l.432). Their preface is dated 'British Museum, 1st October, 1850', title page 'M.DCCC.L.'

Fire of Love written in Latin, translated by Misyn: Misyn's prologue 'I ... have taken this work to translate from Latin into English'; his explicit 'Explicit liber de Incendio Amoris, Ricardi Hampole heremite, translatus in Anglcum instancijs domine Margarete Heslyngton, recluse, per fratrem Ricardum Misyn, sacre theologie bachalaureum, tunc Priorem Lyncolniensem, ordinis carmelitarum, Anno domini Me. CCCCxxxv' (OCR 'Anglcum', 'Me.' for M.); Comper 'he was then Prior of Lincoln and belonged to the Order of the Carmelites'.

Own account, Fire of Love I.15 in Comper's modern spelling of Misyn: 'Forsooth three years, except three or four months, were run from the beginning of the change of my life and of my mind, to the opening of the heavenly door'; 'The door forsooth yet biding open, nearly a year passed until the time in which the heat of everlasting love was verily felt in my heart. I was sitting forsooth in a chapel, and whiles I was mickle ... delighted with sweetness of prayer or meditation, suddenly I felt within me a merry and unknown heat'; 'But first I wavered, for a long time doubting what it could be'; 'half a year, three months and some weeks have out run, until the inshedding and receiving of this heavenly and ghostly sound'; 'Whiles truly I sat in this same chapel, and in the night before supper, as I could, I sang psalms, I beheld above me the noise as it were of readers, or rather singers'; 'I burst out singing what before I said, but forsooth privily, because alone before my Maker.' Page break with running head 'THE FIRE OF LOVE 71' and footnotes between l.5503 and 5516. The brief gives his own intervals, not an editor's total.
Heat, sweetness and song: Horstman 'the 3 phases which he describes as calor, canor, dulcor'; 'The dulcor ... accompanies both the calor and the canor'.

Moving between cells and backbiters (own words): 'I was wont forsooth to seek rest, although I went from place to place. For it is not ill for hermits to leave cells for a reasonable cause'; 'Forsooth the worst backbiters I have had are those which I trusted before as faithful friends.' The Office defends 'frequent change of place'.

Margaret of Anderby, Office Lection VIII: 'this holy man ... had betaken himself to dwell in Richmondshire, it befell that the Lady Margaret, who had once been a recluse at Anderby in the diocese of York'; 'he was wont to instruct her in the art of loving God'; 'as long as I shall remain in this mortal life thou shalt never again suffer the torment of this illness'; 'when the courses of several years had passed, the same illness ... returned to her. Therefore the recluse sent for the goodman aforesaid, and asked him to hasten quickly on horseback to the house of the nuns at Hampole ... where the said Richard at that time led a solitary life'; 'he learnt that the saint was dead to this world; and after diligently inquiring the hour of his passing, he found that the aforesaid illness had returned to the recluse shortly after the hour of Richard's departure'; 'afterwards the recluse betook herself to Hampole where the holy body of the said hermit was given burial'. Told as the Office's account.

Recluse gloss: Horstman calls the Form of Living's addressee 'Margareta anachorita'; Forshall-Madden 'dame Margaret Kirkby, a recluse'. The gloss 'a woman who lived shut in a cell' is the narrator's plain definition of recluse.

Horstman identifies the Margarets: '“Margareta reclusa apud Anderby” (Vita), “Margareta anachorita, dilecta sua discipula” (Form of living), the Margret Kirkby mentioned in the Prologue (by a later poet) to his English commentary of the Psalms'; 'the beautiful “Form of living” addressed (in most Mss) to Margaret'; 'Whether the Cecil to whom the Form of living is addressed in Ms. Rawl., was also a friend of his, cannot be made out.' Forshall-Madden: 'dame Margaret Kirkby, a recluse, probably at Hampole'.

Hampole: Horstman 'he removed to Hampole, and there stayed during the remainder of his life ... The place was a Cistercian nunnery ... He there continued his solitary life, having his cell near or in the grounds of the nunnery'; Comper 'The nuns, to whom Richard ministered and with whom he died, belonged to a well-known Cistercian House at Hampole'; Benson in Comper 'Hampole is still a tiny hamlet, about seven miles distant from Doncaster'.

Day of death: Horstman 'He died on the 29th of September 1349'; 'He died, after several years' residence at Hampole, on the 29th of September 1349, probably of the pestilence'. The day and the cause are Horstman's.
Burial at Hampole: Horstman 'He was buried at Hampole, and by the nuns regarded as a saint and their patron'; the Office 'Hampole where the holy body of the said hermit was given burial'.

Form of Living, Hodgson's modern English: 'Lo, Margaret, I have told thee shortly the Form of Living, and how thou mayst come to perfection'; 'Love is a burning yearning after GOD, with a wonderful delight and certainty.' (brief prints 'God'). Hodgson's title page 'London: Thomas Baker, 72, Newman Street, W. 1910.'; 'The rendering is made from the texts printed by Professor Horstman'.

English Psalter verses, Bodl. Laud 286, 'of the time of Henry the Sixth' per Forshall-Madden: 'Glosed the Sauter that sues here, in Englysch tong sykerly, / At a worthy recluse prayer, cald dame Merget Kyrkby'; 'That ly3t at Hampole in surte, at Richards own berynes, / That he wrote with his hondes, to dame Merget Kyrkby, / Aud ther it ly3t in cheyn bondes, in the same nonery' (OCR 'Aud'); 'Copyed has this Sauter ben, of yuel men of Lollardry, / And afturward hit has bene sene, ympyd in with eresy.' Editors' summary: 'the work was undertaken at the request of dame Margaret Kirkby, a recluse, probably at Hampole; that the autograph copy of the author was still remaining at the nunnery, attached by chains to his tomb ... and that many copies in ordinary use had been corrupted by the Lollards.'

Psalter given to Wyclif: Forshall-Madden 'led Humphrey Wanley to ascribe the more compendious comment to Wycliffe himself in his younger days', concluding it 'represents substantially the original of Rolle'. Arnold: 'in the same catalogue the well-known Commentary on the Psalms, beginning ‘Grete haboundaunce of gostly comfort,’ is ascribed to Wyclif, whereas it has been shown with abundant evidence by the editors of the Wycliffite versions of the Bible (Preface, p. iv) to be the work of Richard Rolle, commonly called Hampole'; 'Bishop Bale's catalogue'; bibliography 'Bale, John, Illustrium Majoris Brltafiniae [OCR] Scriptorum Summarium 1548 and 1559.'

Canticles: Arnold 'down to the end of the seventh canticle, a genuine work of Richard Hampole, retouched in certain MSS. by a Lollard hand, but that the five remaining canticles are a later addition, made either by Wyclif himself, or by his school.'

Lollards as Wyclif's followers: Arnold, of the Lollard canticle passages, 'passages which only Wyclif or one of his disciples could have composed'. Forshall-Madden title: 'made from the Latin Vulgate by John Wycliffe and his followers'.

claims.claim: The sickness and the curate, Long Text ch. III in Warrack's modern spelling: 'I understood by my reason and by my feeling of my pains that I should die'; 'My Curate was sent for to be at my ending, and by that time when he came I had set my eyes, and might not speak. He set the Cross before my face and said: _I have brought thee the Image of thy Maker and Saviour: look thereupon and comfort thee therewith_.'; 'it was all dark about me in the chamber, as if it had been night, save in the Image of the Cross whereon I beheld a common light'; 'And in this [moment] suddenly all my pain was taken from me'. Warrack's italics marks (underscores) dropped in the brief; the brief puts its comma outside the marks, where the file has a colon.

Short Text parallel (Harford's modern spelling): 'they that were with me sent for the parson my curate to be at mine ending. He came, and a child with him ; and brought a cross ... The parson set the cross before my face, and said, " Daughter, I have brought thee the image of thy Saviour.'

Date of the showings: Long Text ch. II 'These Revelations were shewed to a simple creature unlettered, the year of our Lord 1373, the Thirteenth day of May.' Sloane spelling in Warrack's note: 'shewed to a simple creature that cowde no letter the yeere of our Lord 1373 the xiij day of may.' Paris: 'the yer of our Lord a thousande and thre hundered and lxxiii the xiii Daie of May.'
Her own account, in Warrack's modern spelling: Warrack's edition of the Sloane text, introduction signed '_May_ 1901', title page 1901; of Sloane spelling Warrack prints only notes and footnotes.
She never names herself: Warrack 'Julian mentions neither her name not [sic] her state in life; she is "the soul," the "poor" or "simple" soul that the Revelation was shewed to'.

Copyist's heading of the Short Text, Harford's modern spelling: 'INTRODUCTION, BY THE COPYIST / HERE is a vision, showed by the goodness of God to a devout woman, and her name is Julian, that is recluse at Norwich, and yet is on life, anno domini, Mccccxiij.' OCR line breaks without hyphen at 'good / ness' and 'Nor / wich'.

Recluse/anchoress gloss: Harford 'a recluse, or anchoress, in a cell attached to the church of St Julian, Norwich'; Cressy's 1670 preface: 'her profession, which was of the strictest sort of solitary livers ; being inclosed all her life (alone) within four walls'.

Harford printed the Short Text after its purchase in 1909: 'The MS. was then lost to public notice till 1909, when it was bought by the British Museum at Lord Amherst's sale'; 'The Amherst MS., here for the first time printed'. Harford's 1911 date rests on the file header (host metadata); no in-text line gives it, so the brief does not use it.

1413 against 1442: Harford 'It seems to have been seen by Francis Blomefield before the middle of the eighteenth century ... By a curious mistake he gives the date in the introduction (see below p. 16) as "Mccccxlij," for "Mccccxiij," thus giving the Lady Julian's age at that time as 100, instead of 71. This error has misled all later writers upon Lady Julian.' Warrack quotes Blomefield's copy of the title: 'Here es a Vision shewed by the godenes of God to a devoute Woman: and her name is Julian, that is recluse at Noryche, and yett is on life, Anno Domini mccccxlii.' Warrack follows it: 'the old Manuscript says that she "was yet in life" in 1442'; '"yet in life"--as if in great age--in 1442'. Harford also writes that she 'was still living in 1413'.

Age: Long Text 'And when I was thirty years old and a half, God sent me a bodily sickness'; Short Text 'AND when I was thirty winters old and a half'. Warrack: 'This would make her birth-date about the end of 1342'. Harford 'From the internal evidence we learn that she was born about 1342'. Underhill 'Julian of Norwich was born in 1343'; Underhill-H '(1343-c. 1413)'.
claims.witness: WARRACK (julian-of-norwich_revelations-of-divine-love_warrack1901.txt) l.2150-2151, 444-445; HARFORD (julian-of-norwich_comfortable-words-for-christs-lovers_harford1911.txt) l.621-622, 232-233; COMPER (rolle_fire-of-love-and-mending-of-life_comper1914.txt) l.159; UNDERHILL-H (hilton_scale-of-perfection_underhill1923.txt) l.66

claims.claim: The three gifts: 'Which creature [had] afore desired three gifts of God. The First was mind of His Passion; the Second was bodily sickness in youth, at thirty years of age; the Third was to have of God's gift three wounds'; 'freely desiring that sickness [to be] so hard as to death'; 'the wound of very contrition, the wound of kind compassion, and the wound of steadfast longing toward God'.

The hazel-nut: 'Also in this He shewed me a little thing, the quantity of an hazel-nut, in the palm of my hand; and it was as round as a ball. I looked thereupon with eye of my understanding, and thought: _What may this be?_ And it was answered generally thus: _it is all that is made._'

Sin and 'all shall be well': 'afore this time often I wondered why by the great foreseeing wisdom of God the beginning of sin was not letted'; 'answered by this word and said: _It behoved that there should be sin;[1] but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well._' Warrack's footnote mark [1] after 'sin;' is left out of the quotation. Cressy's 1670 text reads 'Sin is behovely' (CRESSY l.2998).

Unlettered: Long Text in Warrack 'a simple creature unlettered,[1]' with footnote '[1] "that cowde no letter" = unskilled in letters.' Sloane spelling 'a simple creature that cowde no letter'. Sloane title, in Warrack's postscript: 'The Sloane MS. is entitled "Revelations to one who could not read a Letter, Anno Dom. 1373,"'. The brief tells the Sloane 'cowde no letter' in modern words ('knew no letter').

Short Text on being a woman, Harford's modern spelling: 'But God forbid that ye should say, or take it so, that I am a teacher, for I mean not so — no, I meant never so. For I am a woman unlearned,13 feeble and frail' (OCR '13' is the footnote mark; Harford's footnote 'b MS. leued.'); 'But, because I am a woman, should I therefore leave [it alone], that I should not tell you the goodness of God, since I saw in the same time that it is His will that it be known ?' The brief paraphrases the second passage without quotation marks.

Which version first: Harford 'In the opinion of the present Editor it is what might be called the " first edition " of the Revelations, and the longer form is the outcome of the twenty years' subsequent meditation ... It has been suggested that it was abbreviated from them : it is here maintained that they were expanded from it.'

Love was His meaning, Long Text ch. LXXXVI: 'And from that time that it was shewed I desired oftentimes to learn what was our Lord's meaning. And fifteen years after, and more, I was answered in ghostly understanding, saying thus: _Wouldst thou learn thy Lord's meaning in this thing? Learn it well: Love was His meaning.' Footnote marks [2] and [3] after 'learn' dropped. Twenty years: 'For, twenty years after the time of the Shewing, save three months, I had teaching inwardly'.

Showings are sixteen and the long text has two versions held: 'Now have I told you of Fifteen Revelations'; 'the good Lord shewed the Sixteenth [Revelation] on the night following'. Harford: the recovered version is 'very much shorter than the type of text represented by' the Paris and Sloane MSS.

Place: Harford 'a recluse, or anchoress, in a cell attached to the church of St Julian, Norwich'; Blomefield quoted by Warrack: 'It is in connection with the old Church of St Julian in the parish of Conisford, outlying Norwich' (Warrack's words) and 'In the east part of the churchyard stood an anchorage in which an ankeress or recluse dwelt till the Dissolution'.

Blomefield on 1393: 'In 1393 Lady Julian, the ankeress here was a strict recluse, and had two servants to attend her in her old age. This woman was in these days esteemed one of the greatest holiness.' Blomefield is eighteenth-century per Harford l.186-188 ('before the middle of the eighteenth century').

Manuscripts: 'This English book exists in two Manuscripts: No. 30 of the Bibliothèque Nationale, Paris ... and No. 2499 _Sloane_, in the British Museum.' Paris explicit: 'Explicit liber Revelationem Julyane anatorite [sic] Norwyche cujus anime propicietur Deus'.

Sloane scribe's warning: 'And beware thou take not on thing after thy affection and liking, and leve another: for that is the condition of an heretique. But take every thing with other.' Warrack assigns the postscript to a scribe.

Cressy's print: 'The earliest printed edition of Julian's book was prepared by the Benedictine Serenus de Cressy, and published in 1670 by permission of his ecclesiastical Superior, the Abbot of Lambspring'; 'it was re-printed in 1843'; 'A modernised version taken from the Sloane MS. was published, with a preface, by Henry Collins in 1877'.

Tersteegen and Poiret: 'Tersteegen, who, in his _Auserlesene Beschreibungen Heiliger Seelen_, gives a long extract from Julian's book (vol. iii. p. 252, 3rd ed. 1784), mentions in his preface that he had seen "in the Library of the late Poiret" an old Manuscript'; 'Pierre Poiret, author of several works on mystical theology, died in 1719 near Leyden'; 'Poiret himself refers thus to Julian ... giving to her name the asterisk denoting greatness: "_Julianae Matris Anachoretae, Revelationes de Amore Dei. Anglice. Theodidactae, profundae, ecstaticae._" (... Amsterdam, 1702.)'

Mother Juliana: Dodd's catalogue quoted in Cressy's 1843 reprint: 'Sixteen Revelations of Divine Love shewed to a devout servant of our Lord called Mother Juliana, a devout anchorete of Norwich'; 1670 title page OCR 'Jttotfjer Juliana, AN ANCHORETE OF NORWICH'. Warrack: 'S. de Cressy was probably the originator of the designation "Mother Juliana." The old name was _Julian_.'
Lady Julian: Harford 'the Lady Julian's age', 'Lady Julian deserves to rank high amongst the great mystics of the world'; Blomefield 'Lady Julian, the ankeress'.

Underhill: 'Julian, the exquisitely human yet profoundly meditative anchoress, whose ‘Revelations of Divine Love’ are perhaps the finest flower of English religious literature'. Underhill edited Hilton's Scale, title page 1923.

Julian Lampet: Warrack 'In _Carrow Abbey_, by Walter Rye (privately printed, 1889), is given a list of Wills, in which the name of the Lady Julian Lampet frequently occurs as a legatee between the years 1427 (Will of Sir John Erpingham) and 1478 (Will of William Hallys)'; 'the identity of the "Lady Julian, recluse at Norwich," with the Lady Julian Lampet, though it has naturally been suggested, is surely an impossibility'; Blomefield 'in 1428 Lady Julian Lampet was anchoress there' (Carrow); Carrow 'consisted of a prioress and nine (afterwards twelve) Benedictine black nuns' and 'was always in the liberty of the City'. Bury will of John Baret, 1463: 'Itm I yeve and beqwete to Dame Julyan Lampet, ancresse of Carrowe, xx d.'

Dalgairns: title page 'With an Essay on The Spiritual Life of Mediaeval England by the Rev. J. B. DALGAIRNS, Priest of the Oratory'; publishers' note: the 1870 reprint of Cressy's text appeared 'with an introduction by Father Dalgairns'. His view: 'It appears, however, most probable that she is the Juliana Lampit to whom a knight ... left a legacy in his will in 1424 ... as she appears to have died in 1443, she must have lived to be a hundred.'

Warrack's guesses: 'Julian, no doubt, was of gentle birth, and she would probably be sent to the Convent of Carrow for her education. There she would receive from the Benedictine nuns the usual instruction in reading, writing, Latin, French, and fine needlework'; 'It is most likely that Julian received at Carrow the consecration of a Benedictine nun'. Harford: 'Of external or historical evidence for Lady Julian's life we have none that can be relied on.'
Harford's edition is of 'the recently discovered manuscript (Brit. Mus. Addit. 37790)', per the file title; the in-text basis is l.198-202 (bought 1909 at Lord Amherst's sale).

claims.claim: Brief opening: on 13 February 1327 Eckhart climbed the preaching seat in the friars' church at Cologne, preached to the people, had Brother Conrad of Halberstadt read his paper, and expounded each article word for word in the mother tongue. DENIFLE-II l.35287-35302: «Acten zum Processe Meister Eckeharts. 631 trecentesimo vicesimo septimo, indictione decima, tertia decima die mensis Februarii hora circa sextam dicte diei, in presentia mei notarii sub- scripti et testium infrascriptorum magister Ekardus, doctor!) sacre theologie, ordinis predicatorum domus Coloniensis, constitutus ascendebat sedem, super qua in ecclesia fratrum dicti ordinis sermo predicari solet, et ibidem predicavit sermonem populo, et ipso sermone finito idem magister vocavit ad se fratrem Conradum de Halverstat dicti ordinis, mandavit ili, ut cartam, quam in manu sua portabat infrascriptam, nomine suo et pro ipso magistro distincte ad intellectum legeret coram populo ibidem presente, et quam primum idem frater unum articulum sive punctum de contentis in ipsa carta legerat, predictus magister illum in materna lingua populo intellective de verbo ad verbum exposuit. Et sic de singulis punctis sive articulis in dicta carta contentis iidem ma-» (OCR 'doctor!)' is a footnote mark; 'ili' for 'illi'; the act names him 'Halverstat', the 24 January act 'Halberstat', l.35088).

Denifle printed the acts from the Vatican originals; volume dated 1886; Denifle a Dominican. DENIFLE-II l.33: «1886.» ; DENIFLE-II l.34965-34967: «Ich publieiere unten nach den Originalen des Vatic. Archivs nur jene Acten, welche sich direct auf Eckehart beziehen, nicht die drei früheren, welche sich mit Nicolaus von Strassburg, der vom» ; DENIFLE-II l.35835: «P. Heinrich Denifle O. P.» (signature 'P. Heinrich Denifle O. P.').

The paper: God called to witness that he always detested every error in faith; he revokes publicly whatever erroneous might be found in what he wrote, said or preached; on the little finger, he spoke of the fingers of the little child Jesus (brief: 'any error that might be found', conditional kept). DENIFLE-II l.35306-35320: «manu propria conscriberem et in formam publicam redigerem meo- que signo consueto signarem. Tenor vero dicte carte talis est: ‘Ego magister Ekardus, doctor saere theologie, protestor ante omnia, deum invocaddo in testem, quod omnem errorem in fide et omnem defor- mitatem in moribus semper?), in quantum michi possibile fuit, sum detestatus, cum hujusmodi errores statui doctoratus mei et ordinis repugna- rent et repugnent. Quapropter si quid erronium (sic!) repertum fuerit in pre- missis?) scriptum per me, dictum vel predicatum, palam vel occulte, ubicumque locorum vel temporum, directe vel indirecte, ex intellectu minus sano vel reprobo, expresse hic revoco publiee coram vobis uni- versis et singulis in presentiarum constitutis, quia id pro non dieto vel scripto exnune haberi volo, specialiter etiam quia male intellectum me audio, quod ego predicaverim, minimum meum digitum creasse omnia, quia illud non intellexi, nec dixi prout verba sonant, sed dixi de digitis ilius parvi pueri Jhesu?). Et quod aliquid sit in anima, si ipsa tota»

claims.claim: Brief opening, told as the History's account (legend, truth disputed): the History and Life of the Reverend Doctor John Tauler opens in 1340; a Master in Holy Scripture preached often in a certain city; a layman warned three times in his sleep came more than thirty leagues; God gave him to perceive the Master was good-hearted with a good understanding of Scripture 'but was dark as to the light of grace'. WINK l.1743-1766: «of the Reverend Doctor John Tauler. FIRST CHAPTER I N the year of Our Lord 1340, it came to pass, that a Master in Holy Scripture preached oft* times in a certain city, and the people loved to hear him, and his teachings were the talk of the country for many leagues round. Now this came to the ears of a layman who was rich in God’s grace, and he was warned three times in his sleep that he should go to the city where the Master dwelt, and hear him preach. Now that dty was in another country, more than thirty leagues distant. Then the man thought within himself, “ I will go thither and wait to see what God is purposed to do or bring to pass there.” So he came to that city and heard the Master preach five times. Then God gave this man to perceive that the Master was a very loving, gentle, good-hearted man by nature, and had a good understanding of the Holy Scripture, but was dark as to the light of grace ; and the man’s heart»

The History: the Master went up into a pulpit, could not speak a word for weeping; the people said he had become 'a downright fool' (line break 'down- right'). claims.claim: Brief opening, the Life's own account (third person): a Friar Preacher, by birth a Swabian, Servitor of the Eternal Wisdom; a woman 'in poverty and suffering' drew from him 'by confidential questionings' his beginning in the interior life; she wrote it down 'by stealth, so that he knew not of it'; finding out 'this ghostly theft' he 'burnt all of it that was there'; 'a heavenly message from God forbidding it' saved the rest; 'for the most part just as she had written it with her own hand'; 'Many good instructions were also added to it by him, after her death, in her name.' KNOX l.520-558: «Introductory. There was a Friar Preacher in Germany, by birth a Swabian, — may his name be written in the Book of the Living ! — whose desire was to become and to be called a Servitor of the Eter- nal Wisdom. Now it happened that he became acquainted with a holy and illuminated person, who was in poverty and suffering as regards this world. This poor sufferer was a woman ; and she used to beseech the Servitor to tell her something about suffering from his own expe- rience, that her suffering heart might gather strength from it. And she acted thus towards him for a long time. When he came to see her, she drew from him by confidential ques- tionings the manner of his beginning and pro- 6 LIFE OF BLESSED HENRY SUSO. gress in the interior life, as well as certain ex- ercises and sufferings which he had passed through : all which he told her in spiritual con- fidence. As she found comfort and direction in these things, she wrote them down, to be a help for herself and others ; and she did this by stealth, so that he knew not of it. Later on, when he found out this ghostly theft, he re- proved her for it, and, forcing her to give up to him the writing, he burnt all of it that was there. When, however, the rest of it was given to him, and he was going to treat it in like man- ner, he was stopped by a heavenly message from God forbidding it. Thus what follows re- mained unburnt, for the most part just as she had written it with her own hand. Many good instructions were also added to it by him, after her death, in her name.»

If the Lord grant me life I will be here often with you."'; 'But in the same year the beloved Master Gerard ... was taken away from this world'.

The house built there: ch. I is headed 'Of the first founders of the Monastery at Mount St. Agnes, and how Master Gerard Groote first pointed out this place to them'; under 1399 the orchard is 'that very garden that Gerard Groote, long before, pointed out to the Brothers'. The Chronicle's sources, its preface: 'these I have seen with mine own eyes, or have heard from the Elders of our House, or else have gathered from the writings of others.'

Citizen of Deventer, death in 1384: Kempis, 'The venerable Master Gerard, called the "Great," was a citizen of the city of Deventer, born of honourable parents of that same place' (drop-cap 'T' lost); 'In the year of the Lord 1384, on the Feast day of the blessed Bernard the Abbot, and at the fifth hour, after Vespers, Gerard, surnamed Groote, died at Deventer, in the time of the pestilence; he was a venerable man and beloved of God, and the forty-fourth year of his age was nearly done.' Aug. 1381,' is a misprint against the text's 'octogesimo quarto'). 'In a time of plague' keeps Kempis's 'in the time of the pestilence'; Kempis does not say he died of it.

claims.claim: Kempis never saw him: 'Though I did not see Gerard in the flesh, yet have I known in the body divers men who owned discipleship to him, and from these I have often heard of his good deeds'. Kempis, a canon of Mount St Agnes, writes as a member of the movement (FOUNDERS 2064-2075, 'I will begin therefore from that notable and devout preacher'). The Life is hagiography by a disciple of the founders' circle; its miracles and prophecies are told as Kempis's account.

The New Devotion and Grote as its first father: Busch, 'Sicut magister Gerardus Magnus origo fuit et pater primus omnium hominum moderne devocionis huius patrie' (OCR 'omni- um'); Arthur's title 'The Founders of the New Devotion'.

Rich parents, Paris, church posts: Kempis, 'His father's name was Werner Groote, and he was a Schepen and magistrate of the same city; his mother was called Heylwige, and both her husband and she were of high place and mighty in honour and riches'; 'Gerard was sent by his parents to the University of Paris, and being furnished with abundant means'; 'a Master of Arts degree was conferred upon him in the eighteenth year of his age ... he was rewarded with preferment in the Church, and received amongst other benefices a Canonry in the Church of Aix.' Salvarvilla: 'He hath long ago given over all his benefices for God's sake, namely prebends at Utrecht and Aix, and also his patrimony, which was no small one'.

Take him in my stead"'; Busch, 'dominum Florencium Radewini in artibus magistrum in ecclesia Davantriensi vicarium virum illuminatum et devotum omnibus rectorem prefecit et loco sui ut patrem honorandum'.

Close, his own notes: Kempis's heading, 'Resolutions and Intentions set forth by Master Gerard in the name of the Lord, but not confirmed by vows.'; the line, 'Let the root of thy study and the mirror of thy life be these: First, the Gospel of Christ, for therein is the Life of Christ.' Arthur: 'it is obvious from a perusal of the original that the whole is taken from notes made by Gerard himself'.

Preached against vice (card): Kempis, 'because he argued with severity against their own vices and crimes'; the friend's letter, 'hath denounced before clerks and layfolk their wickedness, and maintained wholesome, true, Evangelical and Apostolic doctrine as against heretics, usurers, and clerks that live in concubinage'.
Birth year, editors only: Arthur, 'between 1340, the date of Groote's birth, and 1439'; Opzoomer, 'Hij is in 1340 te Deventer geboren' (OCR 'Hij'', 'ïn').

Letters (card): Acquoy's edition, 'EPISTOLAE XIV'; preface signed 'Scribebam Amstelodami, d. 29 Augusti MDCCCLVII' (OCR 'Angusti'); letter written after the ban, Acquoy: 'postquam ei interdictum erat praedicare'; Grote: 'Sed non datur quies. Nihil penitus scribo, sed objicientibus aliquibus respondeo'. Kempis quotes letters in English, e.g. 'I am ever covetous, yea, more than covetous, of books' and 'Many snarling folk' (OCR 'Manysnarling').

claims.claim: Translations (card): 'He translated two books of John Ruesbroeck from the Teutonic into the Latin tongue, and these are entitled: "Ecce Sponsus" and "De gradibus amoris." Likewise he translated "The Hours of the Blessed Virgin," and certain of the Hours from the Latin into the Teutonic tongue, so that simple and unlearned Laics might have in their mother tongue matter wherewith to occupy themselves in prayer'.

Traces (card): Kempis, 'Some of these disciples were they who dwelt in the Monastery of Windesheim, and also they who with the help of God first founded the house of Agnietenburg near Zwolle'; 'After the death of the venerable Master Gerard Groote, the devotion of faithful persons in Deventer, Zwolle, Kampen and the neighbouring towns began to grow mightily in the Lord, so that in a short time there arose many congregations of men and women that served God, dwelling together in common'. Busch on the sisters: 'sorores in domo magistri Gerardi in Davantria ... de manuum suarum laboribus nendo filando et texendo vite et victus necessaria'; 'horas beate virginis ... materna lingua iuxta magistri Gerardi translacionem ... legere'.

Hermen Sticke (card), the Diepenveen sisters in Middle Dutch: 'Dji eerweerdige mater Salomee was eens eersamen mans dochter, geheyten Hermen Sticke'; 'Op een tijt quam hij daer meyster Gerijt die Groete een sermoen dede'; 'so liet hij rechtevoert achter sijn ruterschap ... ende bekierde hem geheel tot onsen lieven Heren' (OCR 'quam.hij', footnote marks). Told in modern words.

claims.claim: Remembered (card): Salvarvilla, in Kempis's Chronicle, 'Truly he was "The Great," for in his knowledge of all the liberal sciences ... he was second to no one in the world'; 'Master William of Salvarvilla, Cantor at Paris, Archdeacon of Brabant in the Church of Liege, an eminent doctor in theology, compiled the above eulogy from that which he heard from the lips of men worthy of credit, and from his own knowledge of Master Gerard'. Busch copies it: 'Magister Wilhelmus doctor in theologia cantor Parisiensis ita de eo scribit'. Busch reporting Prior John Vos of Heusden ('Venerabilis ergo pater noster lohannes Huesden ... dicens'): 'Magister Gerardus Magnus primus fuit huius nostre reformacionis pater et tocius moderne devocionis origo verusque hiis novissimis temporibus huius nostre terre apostolus'.

Epitaph and Underhill (card): Arthur, 'It is uncertain whether A Kempis was the author of the lines, but from the title "Epitaphium vetus et inconditum" it would seem probable that they are by a different hand'; 'Gerardus Magnus vixit sicut pius agnus, Fecit quod dixit, sicut docuit quoque vixit.' Underhill: 'Gerard Groot, afterwards the founder of the Brothers of the Common Life and hence spiritual ancestor of Thomas a Kempis'.

Turn from the world (card): Kempis's hermit at Cologne, 'the aforesaid hermit, expressly mentioning the name and describing the dress of Gerard, foretold that his conversion should shortly be brought to pass' (told as Kempis's account); Grube, 'Im Jahre 1374 wandte er sich von der Welt ab' (OCR 'Iki'). No year in Kempis's Life or Chronicle (searched '1374', '1372').

Acquoy on the decree (card): 'Ne enim diutius concionaretur, ex episcopi decreto omnibus praeter sacerdotes conciones sacras habere interdictum est ... Accedebat ut ceteri fere omnes mox restituerentur, Gerardus autem, ratione non data, jure concionandi quo diaconi utebantur, privatus maneret' (heavy OCR, cleaned; file: 'diutins eonoionaretor', 'aaeerdotes', 'restitaerentar', 'jnre', 'ntebantinr', 'privatila').

Towns (card): Arthur's Kempis, 'He preached in the chief cities of the diocese of Utrecht, Deventer and Zwolle; in Kempen often, and in Utrecht itself before the assembled clergy; in the country of Holland at Leyden, Delft and Ghent; in Amsterdam (where he delivered his first sermon in the vulgar tongue)'. Busch: 'in Traiecto videlicet Davantria Swollis Campis Amarstordia Amsterdammis Heerlem Gouda Leidis Delft Sutfania' (footnote marks). Kempis's Latin Life is not held (no Pohl volume with the Vita Gerardi).

Ruysbroek companions (card): Chronicle, 'This was he whom Master Gerard Groote visited, together with John, a scholar from Zwolle'; Life, 'He took with him therefore that revered man Master John Cele, the director of the School of Zwolle'; 'There went also with them a faithful and devout layman, named Gerard the shoemaker'. Grunthal: 'John Ruysbroek, a monk and Prior of the Monastery of Grunthal, near Brussels' (OCR 'Sj Prior').

Flowers or roses (card): Kempis, 'So soon as I am come to God, I hope I shall cast down upon you flowers out of Heaven'; Busch, 'tale illis flentibus et merentibus fertur dedisse responsum' and 'rosas vobis de celo in sinus vestros transmittam'. Grube's note compares Kempis's 'quod proiiciam vobis flores de celo'.

Low German writings (card): the tract, headed 'Gherd de groet', opens 'Dit is my ghevraghet, oftet symonia sy, ene stede ot ene prouende te copen in enen beglÜDen convente' (OCR); Langenberg argues for Groote from the contemporary heading, a second witness in Bunderius's catalogue, and style ('So wären zwei äussere Zeugnisse für die Autorschaft Grootes gegeben'). Lay rule: 'Die Laienregel war schon zum Teil gedruckt, als ich sah, dass es die des Dietrich Engelhusen ist'.
